endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Those include recommendations for creating safe and effective systems; algorithmic discrimination protections; data privacy; notice and explanation; and human alternatives, considerations, and fallback.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: In settings where patients may interact directly with AI solutions, such as scheduling assistants or triage support, a simple "Request Human Assistance" option can go a long way toward building trust and accommodating patients who prefer a different experience.

endorsements.title: Human-Centered AI in Crisis Counseling: A Three-Tier Governance Framework
endorsements.quote: Callers must be told immediately they are interacting with an automated system, offered silence as an alternative, and prioritized for human connection according to predefined, service-approved criteria rather than any AI interpretation of clinical state.

endorsements.title: Your robot therapist is not your therapist: understanding the role of AI-powered mental health chatbots
endorsements.quote: Second, if an opt out feature is availed, users should have access to a human therapist who can provide them with the necessary care they need.

endorsements.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chatbots for Depression Management: A New Frontier in Primary Care
endorsements.quote: The use of AI chatbots should enhance rather than replace the human-to-human therapeutic relationship, and patients should have access to human providers for aspects of care that require genuine empathy and emotional support.

endorsements.title: Solidarity or Segregation? ChatGPT Health and US Health Care Disparities
endorsements.quote: Integration should enable warm handoffs to human services, countering the risks of self-rationing and self-medication behaviors described above.

endorsements.title: Generative AI for pre-consultation mental health triage in disorders of gut-brain interaction
endorsements.quote: Paper, telephone, or assisted completion routes are needed for patients with limited digital access, language barriers, low health literacy, or symptom severity that makes extensive questionnaires difficult.

endorsements.title: Generative AI as interactional infrastructure for meaning-centered care in later life
endorsements.quote: Governance should also include a right not to be automated.

endorsements.title: An Evidence-Based Framework for Patient-Facing Artificial Intelligence Integration in the Emergency Department
endorsements.issuer: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
endorsements.quote: PF-AI should always be paired with an equivalent staff-assisted fallback, such as interpreter-supported intake, bedside staff engagement, or standard nondigital workflows, so patients who cannot or do not wish to engage digitally are not excluded.

endorsements.title: Reclaiming the Human Connection in Clinical Care With AI
endorsements.quote: Importantly, all patient-facing AI navigation tools should be designed with the same consent and privacy standards applied to ambient documentation: patients should understand what the AI can and cannot do, how their data is used, and how to reach a human clinician when needed.

evidence.title: Lived Experiences of AI-Mediated Therapeutic Relationships: A Qualitative Exploration of User Attachment to Generative AI Mental Health Chatbots Among Adults
evidence.outcome: Users' experience of dependency and absence of human escalation pathways in mental health chatbots
evidence.effect: Fragile Dependency theme: prolonged use generated attachment anxiety about app discontinuation or data breaches, compounded by absence of human escalation pathways. Authors call for mandatory human handoff protocols.
evidence.quote: prolonged use generated attachment anxiety about potential app discontinuation or data breaches, compounded by absence of human escalation pathways

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether offering patients a human-assistance option during AI interactions improves safety, trust, or access, so this recommendation rests on nine endorsements, seven of them commentaries, and one qualitative hazard study. The hazard study suggests that users of mental health chatbots experience dependency and distress when no human escalation pathway exists.

perspectives.view: No study compares patient-facing AI with and without a human-assistance option. The only empirical study is a qualitative interview study of 37 adults in Nigeria that documents the hazard. Under GRADE conventions the practice has no direct evidence. The nine endorsements, seven commentaries, one guidance document, and one framework, represent expert opinion rather than tested effect.

Interviewees described attachment anxiety about app discontinuation or data breaches, which the authors report was compounded by the absence of human escalation pathways. This suggests a failure mode in which distressed users have no route to a clinician. The study does not show that a handoff option would catch or prevent that harm.

Two endorsements name patients with language barriers, limited digital access, or low health literacy as needing paper, telephone, interpreter-supported, or staff-assisted routes. The single hazard study was conducted in Nigeria and did not report on Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency populations, so the need for these groups is inferred rather than measured.

One guidance document lists human alternatives, considerations, and fallback as a principle alongside safety, discrimination protection, privacy, and notice. The supplied sources present these as recommendations and do not identify a binding federal or state requirement, so adoption currently depends on institutional policy.

The endorsements frame a human option as a matter of trust and of a right not to be automated, and one commentary asks that patients understand how to reach a human clinician when needed. The interview data suggest that patients who lack this route may feel dependent on the tool and anxious about losing it.

commentary.research_gap: No study has measured whether a request-human option changes escalation rates, time to human contact, missed urgent needs, patient trust, or abandonment of care, nor what staffing a fallback service requires at different levels of use. Comparative deployment studies of scheduling, triage, and mental health chatbots with and without human handoff would address this.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The one hazard study enrolled 37 adults in Nigeria and did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy status, so the benefit for these groups, whom two endorsements single out as likely to need non-digital or interpreter-supported alternatives, remains unmeasured.
